unharnessed.meaning: Every instruction survives, including the repeated warning about loud noises, the racehorse speed, the brown versus black bear rules and the tent rule: "If any bear attacks you in your tent, or stalks you and then attacks, do NOT play dead—fight back!"
unharnessed.sense: The few local terms fit: "Getting your tucker will only encourage the bear", "most bears don't want to have a go at you", "Clear out of the area".
unharnessed.authenticity: What Aussie there is sounds natural and unforced; it reads like a ranger talking plainly: "Pick up small kids straight away."
unharnessed.register: Lighter than level 2 asks: mostly plain, casual international English ("Stay still; stand your ground but slowly wave your arms"), with only "tucker", "have a go" and "Clear out" marking it as Australian.
unharnessed.tone: The serious, careful safety tone is kept whole, capitals and all: "Do NOT run or make any sudden movements."
unharnessed.flow: Reads cleanly: "If the bear isn't moving, back off slowly and sideways; that way you can keep an eye on the bear and not trip over."
unharnessed.variety: Very little slang to vary; "tucker" appears only once, while "food" is kept elsewhere, so there is little range.
unharnessed.essence: Unmistakably the park-service bear guidance, in the same order and with the same emphasis.

yarn.meaning: All the instructions survive accurately: "Do NOT drop your pack, because it can protect your back and stop a bear from getting into your tucker." "Help look after others by reporting every bear run-in to a park ranger straight away."
yarn.sense: Most terms fit well: "having a sticky beak" for a curious standing bear, "twig to a group", "put the wind up bears" for intimidating, "egg the bear on". "If a brown/grizzly bear has a go at you" softens a full attack, and "turning into a real drama" undersells escalation.
yarn.authenticity: Sounds like a real Australian ranger: "Pick up the littlies straight away", "make things worse for the next lot", "because there's more of you all up".
yarn.register: Clean, as vulgarity 0 asks, but a notch heavier than level 2: "sticky beak", "twig", "put the wind up", "egg the bear on", "Getting a feed off you" all crowd in.
yarn.tone: Mostly keeps the serious safety tone, but a few casual phrases soften the danger: "stop it turning into a real drama", "If a brown/grizzly bear has a go at you".
yarn.flow: Smooth and natural: "So bears often twig to a group from further away, and because there's more of you all up, groups put the wind up bears too."
yarn.variety: Wide range without repetition: "sticky beak", "littlies", "twig", "egg on", "a feed", "run-in", "cleared off", "bolts".
yarn.essence: Clearly the same safety guide, with the same structure and every rule.

engine.meaning: All content survives, since it is the original almost word for word: "Do NOT allow the bear access to your tucker."
engine.sense: "tucker" fits as food, but "Pick up little fellas immediately" is an odd fit for small children of either sex, and "protecting tucker, cubs, or their space" applies human slang to bear food.
engine.authenticity: "tucker" dropped into otherwise formal US agency prose sounds pasted in: "prevent a bear from accessing your tucker".
engine.register: Left almost entirely untranslated; the only changes are "tucker", "little fellas" and British spellings ("behaviour", "recognise").
engine.tone: The original's serious tone is untouched: "The chances of an attack escalate greatly if she perceives you as a danger to her cubs."
engine.flow: Reads as the original does, apart from jarring joins where slang lands in formal syntax: "Do NOT allow the bear access to your tucker. Getting your tucker will only encourage the bear".
engine.variety: One term, "tucker", repeated four times, plus "little fellas".
engine.essence: Unmistakably the original, as it barely changes it.

unharnessed.quote: Stay still; stand your ground but slowly wave your arms.
unharnessed.original: Remain still; stand your ground but slowly wave your arms.
unharnessed.why: Representative of the text staying plain English rather than taking a light Australian colour; under the level-2 brief.

yarn.quote: If a brown/grizzly bear has a go at you
yarn.original: If you are attacked by a brown/grizzly bear
yarn.why: "has a go at you" can read as a mild set-to; for a grizzly attack it slightly softens the stakes.

yarn.quote: stop it turning into a real drama
yarn.why: Slightly flippant for a dangerous wildlife encounter.

yarn.original: groups are also intimidating to bears
yarn.why: Correct sense, but one of several pieces of slang that push the text past a light level 2.

engine.quote: Do NOT allow the bear access to your tucker. Getting your tucker will only encourage the bear
engine.original: Do NOT allow the bear access to your food. Getting your food will only encourage the bear
engine.why: A single slang word swapped repeatedly into formal agency prose; it reads as find-and-replace, not Australian.
"little fellas" is gendered and slightly odd for small children in a safety rule; "littlies" or "kids" fits better.

engine.quote: Once a bear has noticed you and is paying attention to you, additional strategies can help prevent the situation from escalating.
engine.original: Once a bear has noticed you and is paying attention to you, additional strategies can help prevent the situation from escalating.
engine.why: Left untranslated, like most of the text; well under the level-2 brief.

summaries.unharnessed: Accurate, clear and tonally right, but closer to plain-English simplification than to a level-2 Aussie touch.
summaries.yarn: The most authentically Australian of the three and fully accurate, a bit heavier than level 2 with a couple of phrases that soften the danger.
summaries.engine: The original with a word-swap or two; faithful and correctly toned by default, but barely Australian.
